title: Sequels Don’t Ruin Original Films. Ever.

commenti.body: Your post seems to posit that we're not allowed to be mad at studios for their bad decisions. If people don't speak up, they'll just keep making shitty sequels forever. Some months it feels like Hollywood is becoming mostly sequels. So because I don't want that to happen, I implore anyone reading this to get MORE MAD next time a dumb sequel is announced and complain more, so that hopefully it will translate to more original movies.
[removed]

They definitely matter to an extent. They change the cultural context for a movie.

It’s sort of like how my response to a painting is going to be different depending on whether it is hung up in the Metropolitan Museum of Art or my local McDonalds.

I don't really care about sequels ruining the legacy of the source material (though it is annoying to see a bad sequel get made for a property you love), I care about shitty sequels getting made in lieu of actually good movies.  

It's a waste.  A waste of resources, money, time, manpower on movies that are *worthless* and will not be remembered.  

We cannot make infinite movies; we are limited by how resource-intensive they are & it is infuriating how big studios keep green-lighting cash grab *CRAP* versus anything that is *AT LEAST* a tiny bit original or heart-felt.  It sucks, & us normal people who love movies but have no power in this industry are allowed to be annoyed.  We're allowed to be critical.  That's the whole thing about art. 

Especially when these studios get indignant & act like we're the problem for not hand over our hard-earned dollars for garbage.

I agree as long as the new one isn’t Battlefield Earth bad. I didn’t completely love the Disney Star Wars but it never made the old ones worse for me. To many, however, it appears to have ruined star wars entirely.

This is almost comically wrong. Studios fear nothing more than silence and indifference. It's the kiss of death for any production.

The more loudly you complain about something, the more free publicity you are inadvertently giving it. Going on endlessly about how bad a sequel is, is basically keeping the franchise alive and making sure sooner or later someone will try to profit from it again. Don't want mediocre sequels? Ignore them, don't watch them, don't talk about them, put your attention elsewhere. 

Sadly, moaning and getting MAD is more juicy. And because Hollywood understands human nature, they continue to profit from it by churning out low effort products and letting the haters sell it for them.
This. Silence is consent.

A strong example of this is Disney's Star Wars or the video game Last of Us 2. The cast and crew deserved all the hate from the fan community. Disney/NaughtyDog also made up fake rumors about Marie Tran, Mose Ingram, and Laura Bailey to make the real fans look bad

I agree. Ultimately, what really counts is showing up at festivals and for original / personal films. And not give them cash for the seventeenth shitty sequel of a film just so you can rant about it online. Because that's just a win for the studio. Always has been. And bad for the original films you will probably not watch because you opted for the popular one you knew you wouldn't like anyway. (Not talking about anyone here, just something you keep seeing online.)
If you make crap movies , you deserve all the hate that comes with it. Sorry for introducing to reality.

The hangover was at the time a classic film that would still be talked about if the sequels didn’t completely ruin what the first accomplished. The sequels literally ruined the cult following of the film. 

Is that a minority example, sure, but the sequels ruined the legacy of the first film.
I don't know if I'd go so far as to call prequel fans "people"
Prequel fans and Disney fans all deserve the kathy griffin treatment. If you do wrong by the fans, you deal with the consequences.

Where are you seeing the OP posit that people aren’t allowed to be mad at studios? They didn’t write anything about anybody being allowed or not allowed to do *anything*. The bizarre idea that disagreement equates to censorship is becoming all too common.

Yeah I find it hard to understand these people who get so mad about movies that come out, especially sequels and remakes. On one hand I think they are just really caught up in the marketing and the drama, basically the social aspect of posting online about it. On a deeper level though, I think they really idealize Hollywood and are outraged to realize that it all comes down to dollars and cents. 

If you already know that mass culture has been mostly lowest common denominator for the past 100 years, then you won’t be mad at any particular fad or trend. Then you can see that there have also been many diamonds in the rough, and if you try to go through all the good stuff out there it’s more than you can reasonably watch in a lifetime.

Star Wars is a unique case. Problem with Disney is that they killed the Expanded Universe for their new universe. And this is a big problem insofar that the EU allowed for much more creativity and ideas than Disney's timeline. Plus of course that we (Star Wars fans) care for the universe. I for one criticize it because there is still potential, and the masterfully done Andor shows that sometimes stuff gets done right.

It's not even that the EU was inherently better in the sequel era. It got really weird and murky there too, just on a more crazy and less predictable level. But it still had so much more maturity and personality because it wasn't planned like Marvel films or whatever. It was rewarding because you had novels, comics of all kind and could just enjoy what you want. It got us quite a few phenomenal works in Star Wars, and I mean *extraordinary*. It's a bit annoying that with Disney many suffer the "newest stuff first" syndrome and ignore the actual good, but "inofficial" content which is just... market rhetoric people feed into, at the end of the day. But time will tell which stories will remain and which will be forgotten. It has always been so. Still kinda hurts how Disney bleeds the franchise dry, and hard to comprehend what with the limitless potential of the universe.

The problem is not that there are many mediocre shows now, it's that Disney builds upon these shows and you can't go back from them. It's not like an unasked random sequel for Psycho or Alien which can suck or... rock. It's a universe that has been established as one where many writers and artists can tell their story, it's like a modern pool of fairytales, which is why its fanfiction community is so incredibly alive. But Disney does not tackle it as such, it makes the same mistake that Hollywood keeps on doing as of the past decade and tries to make everything multiverse, and thereby every work ultimately loses its own personality. It's not healthy and in the long run could very well be the death of the franchise as it is. Maybe for the better. Because if you handle your IP like that, and everything needs to be watched, while you keep shitting out content, sooner or later people will just take a break. It's simply too overwhelming.

And then the frustration of Star Wars fans of course comes from the fact that the executives have time and time again either not listened to the criticism, outright said it's disingenuous and toxic because they focus on twitter voices and the likes, or even done shit like Hidalgo making fun of a famous fan and fan creator because he cried tears of happiness for a show that hit all the right marks. It's not... a nice sphere. It's very conflicting.

Personally, I just focus on what I enjoy, read the old, great stuff, play KotOR 2 and am always ready when Claudia Gray writes another nice (YA-ish but great) banger and do not support them by watching their shit just because it says "Star Wars". And, as I said, with time this obsession about what is "important" will end in people just going to what is deemed good. Most hyped and successful films are, as history of Box Offices shows, products of their time and only in part what will actually be remembered of that time. But even then, just support work that is crafted with passion and avoid films that are clearly just calculated entertainment products - unless that entertainment product is actually fun for you, then why be dogmatic? That's about it.

No, sequels don’t ruin the originals, but yes, I take issue with the way my loyalty to the originals has been used against me, when it comes to sitting through way too much sequel bullshit.

We have been drowning in sequels and franchises for so long and it's more important than ever to champion new, original, stand-alone movies. I find it odd that anyone feels the need to defend or champion the idea of sequels.

That exact situation happens all the time. Completed films with huge budgets have even been pulled at post-production.

I mean, by definition it’s hard to divorce a sequel from the original. Unless it’s a spinoff or soft reboot it’s directly taking the story and ideas from the previous installment and expanding on them. Sometimes in a good way (*Bladerunner 2049*), sometimes in a god fucking awful way (*The Last Jedi*). So yes, people who are passionate about the first film get upset when a sequel feels out of place, or ruins the tone or destroys their favorite character. Entries in a franchise, unfortunately don’t exist in a vacuum and some franchises like *Star Wars* seem to have a different writer and/or director w/each entry, so there’s no uniting vision, there’s retcons, one writer takes the story left, then the next one says ‘nah, fuck it, this one’s turning right’ and now the stories a mess.
Yes! It’s like The Godfather or The Dark Knight is lesser than for some reason. It was and it still is a great movie on its own merit.

The original context being lost or muddied by subsequent installments will absolutely affect the legacy of a work. 

I'm not saying that this is always bad, but it is true that the legacy becomes complicated, and can become unsettled permanently: It is almost inherent that works which become a franchise create differing of opinions that will each - seperately, and competitively - try to take over the narriative of a work's legacy; making it contentious (worst case scenerio), or uncertain (best case scenerio).

I suppose there are films like the Exorcist which escape this in a mainstream context - though newer installments seem to want to change the original's status as an outlier in this argument - but even deeper fanbases of this film franchise can have lost sight of the original context.
